newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary BUX ends at new record of 6,994.30 pts.
newsitem.headline: Hungary BUX ends at new record of 6,994.30 pts.

text.p: Hungarian share prices powered ahead on Thursday, benefiting from expectations of lower domestic interest rates, U.S. orders brought forward and an approaching NATO summit in Madrid, traders and analysts said.
The BUX index finished at a second successive new high, a preliminary 6,994.30 points, up 123.73. Volume of traded stocks and compensation coupons amounted to 1,579,345 units.
"The coming NATO summit and overseas investors who brought their purchases forward due to a July 4 holiday, were behind the rise," said Attila Berecz of Raiffeisen Securities.
Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic are expected to get invitations to join NATO at a Madrid summit next week.

The fact that the U.S. Fed left its rates steady on Thursday might have contributed to the rise to some extent, Berecz said, but added he explained it by the NATO summit and orders brought forward rather than by steady Fed rates.
Berecz said the fact that the Thai market firmed eight percent on Thursday after a decision to float the baht showed that investors turn their attention towards emerging markets.
BUX futures finished above Wednesday's settlement prices but rose at a slower pace than at the cash market, traders said.

"Interest content has narrowed, the market probably feels that the end of the year is still far away, and nobody expects this pace of rise (on the cash market) to be maintained," Berecz said. "Futures investors are more cautious."
September BUX contain an around nine percent interest compared to around 12 percent on Wednesday.

On the cash market shares were rising despite a denial by privatisation agency APV Rt on Thursday that oil company MOL, OTP Bank, and meat processor Pick would qualify for a payout of privatisation revenues under a 1989 law.
MOL finished at 4,190 forints, up five. OTP rallied to a new record high of 5,270 forints before closing at 5,215, up 65. Pick ended at 14,500 forints, up 100.
An analyst said fresh capital was reaching the Hungarian market, bolstering prices.

"It (the rise) is got to do with interest rate expectations, I guess," said Sara Zervos, emerging market strategist at BZW in London. "If people perceive lower interest rates then the market always reacts positively."
"And there's always money still pouring in from foreigners and this keeps on supporting prices," Zervos added.
